lesson.title: Everyone You Actually Care About: Defining a Population
lesson.summary: This section defines a statistical population as the complete group a researcher wants to learn about, using a school of 1,200 students as a running example for the sections that follow.
lesson.body:
Statistics, as the first section of this course explained, is the science of collecting and analyzing data in order to answer questions. Nearly every statistical question has a target: a specific group of individuals the question is actually about. That complete group, every single individual you would want to include if you could, is called the population. A population is not necessarily a group of people. It could be every lightbulb produced by a factory in a year, every lake in a state, or every transaction processed by a bank in a month. What makes a group a population, in the statistical sense, is simply that it is the entire collection the researcher wants to draw conclusions about.

Populations can be enormous, and that size is often exactly why they cause practical problems. Imagine Lincoln High School, a school with 1,200 enrolled students, and suppose a researcher wants to know how many hours of sleep the typical Lincoln High student gets on a school night. The population here is clearly defined: all 1,200 currently enrolled students. In theory, if the researcher had unlimited time and cooperation, every one of those 1,200 students could be surveyed, and the result would describe the population completely and exactly. Surveying an entire population this way is called a census. In practice, censuses are often expensive, slow, or simply impossible, which is exactly the problem the next section addresses.

Precisely defining the population is one of the most important and most frequently overlooked steps in any statistical study. If the researcher actually wants to know about sleep habits of American teenagers in general, but only ever measures Lincoln High students, the population being studied is really just Lincoln High, not American teenagers as a whole, and any conclusions should not be stretched beyond that narrower group without strong justification. A huge share of misleading statistics in the real world comes not from bad arithmetic, but from describing a narrow population, like customers of one particular store, as if it were a much broader one, like all consumers everywhere.

As a small worked illustration of population size mattering, suppose Lincoln High's 1,200 students break down as exactly 625 students who identify as female and 575 who identify as male. The proportion of the population that is female is found by dividing 625 by the total population size, 1,200, which gives 625 divided by 1,200, equal to approximately 0.521, or 52.1 percent. Because this calculation used every single member of the population, no estimation is involved. It is not an approximation of the truth. It is the exact truth about that population, on that day, for that specific characteristic.

Since surveying a full population of 1,200 students is often impractical, researchers instead study a smaller, more manageable group drawn from that population. That smaller group, and how it relates back to the full population defined here, is the subject of the next section.
